analysis.one_liner: Directs federal agencies to shift credit, guarantee, and insurance risk to private markets.
analysis.headline: The House Oversight Committee approved the bill 24-15 on November 20, 2024, but the House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill declares it U.S. policy to shift the credit, guarantee, and insurance risk held by federal agencies to private companies "at market terms." Every agency running a federal loan, guarantee, or insurance program — including Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac while under government conservatorship — would have to publish a strategy and implementation plan for moving that risk to private markets, identify legal barriers to doing so, and report the estimated costs or savings. Transfers could not directly raise any individual's fees or premiums, and the bill excludes Social Security and Medicare. It creates a new regular business for private insurers, reinsurers, and investors who would take on — and charge for — risk the government currently holds cheaply.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, private insurers, reinsurers, investment banks, and asset managers would gain a large, recurring new market: taking over the credit and insurance risk behind federal programs and mortgage guarantees, priced at market rates. The bill's stated purpose is protecting taxpayers from catastrophic losses by putting that risk on private balance sheets.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each agency with credit, guarantee, or insurance programs to publish a plan, at least every five years, for transferring that risk to private markets at market terms, and to identify any law or regulation standing in the way.
Requires private entities that accept transferred risk to report claims and payments back to the agency, and requires OMB to report to Congress on the volume, savings, and costs of the transfers.

Bars agencies from making any transfer that would directly result in an increased fee, premium, or other cost to an individual, and excludes the Social Security Administration and Medicare from the mandate.

analysis.who_pays: The government would pay private firms market prices to take on risk that the federal government currently finances at near-Treasury rates, so the cost of running federal insurance and guarantee programs would tend to rise over time. Those costs surface indirectly — through program budgets and, eventually, the pricing of mortgages and other credit — since the bill only bans direct increases to individual fees. Taxpayers also remain exposed in a crisis, because private risk markets historically retract exactly when losses spike.

drawbacks.text: Private capital charges more to bear risk than the government effectively pays to bear it itself, so systematically transferring federal credit and insurance risk "at market terms" tends to raise the long-run cost of federal programs; the bill's ban covers only transfers that directly increase an individual's fee or premium, not indirect costs.

Private risk markets pull back in downturns, so in exactly the crisis scenarios the bill's cost analysis contemplates — years of higher-than-normal defaults — the risk can flow back to the government, weakening the federal capacity to keep credit and insurance flowing when it is needed most.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's taxpayer-protection framing has a real basis: concentrating federal guarantee and insurance risk on the government's books means taxpayers absorb catastrophic losses, as the 2008 housing collapse showed. But the mechanism runs through new revenue for the private risk-transfer industry at market prices above the government's own cost of funds, and the protections offered — a ban on direct fee increases and 60-day public comment — do not address the indirect way those higher costs reach borrowers. As written, the bill's clearest and most durable beneficiaries are the financial firms that would take on the risk, not the taxpayers it says it protects.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Oversight Committee 24-15 in November 2024, but the House never brought it to the floor, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Byron Donalds (R-FL) introduced the bill on July 15, 2024, joined by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL) as its sole cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, which held a markup on November 20, 2024 and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute by a vote of 24-15.
No further action appears in the record: the bill was never scheduled for a House floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, taxpayers kept the government's current low-cost direct holding of federal credit and insurance risk, while the private insurers, reinsurers, and investors who would have gained a new government-supplied market got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; the private risk-transfer industry lost out

sides.party_line_note: The committee advanced it 24-15, but the provided record does not show how the votes split by party; the bill's only named Democratic supporter was its cosponsor, Rep. Krishnamoorthi.

industries.note: The bill would make private markets the permanent, mandated channel for federal credit, guarantee, and insurance risk, creating recurring demand for these firms' services at market prices above the government's own cost of funds. Those higher costs reach the public indirectly through program budgets and credit pricing, since only direct individual fee increases are banned.

Firms that structure and trade risk-transfer instruments would gain a steady pipeline of government risk to package and hold. Their earnings depend on charging more for risk than the government pays to keep it, a cost the public ultimately absorbs.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (mortgage guarantee operations)
industries.note: While in conservatorship, the two mortgage-finance giants would be required to move guarantee risk to private investors, shrinking the guarantee book that generates their income and advancing the broader push to re-privatize them. Homebuyers would face whatever pricing private investors charge for the risk the GSEs give up.
